From early childhood, I took to hobbies like video games and reading because I could have all the fun all on my own, with little or no need to interact with other people; in those instances where team based play was necessary or encouraged, most games had robust offline content that often, in the case of a game like, say, Diablo 2, were nearly identical to the online counterpart - if I'd had enough of other people for the day, I could simply kick them out of my game, close it off, and enjoy it as a single player experience. Generally, communication was kept to a minimum among randos, unless you were going over drops and proposing trades. Hell, even a game like Age of Empires required minimal amounts of communication for a casual multiplayer game.

For me, those were the glory days of gaming; the times when I'd put away my homework, finish dinner with my parents, and seclude myself away from the world to play. Socializing all day in school was mentally exhausting. The few friends I had, I really only kept around because I didn't want to be seen as a social outcast (much to my dismay, I still got my fair share of bullying, but that's not the point here). Whatever energy I had to expend keeping up the appearances of not wanting to just barricade myself in a room and play video games was alleviated by the time I got to spend alone, doing the thing I loved. It's 2016 now, and my love for "antisocial" hobbies hasn't changed - rather, video gaming itself has changed, and I'm painfully aware that what I'm expressing here is the kind of sentiment you'd hear out of a "I liked [band] before they went mainstream" Seattle fucknut hipster, but deep in my heart of hearts, I really did like gaming more before it went mainstream; it's not just the incursion of culture critics like Jack Thompson and Anita Sarkeesian, it's the entire premise of gaming as a social activity as a whole as it has become mainstream that has started to change how I feel - or maybe better phrased, connect with games.

I'm sure we're all old enough here to remember the days of GameFAQs being the premier place to go for guides on everything from character building, story arcs within a game, 100% walkthroughs, and compendiums of custom Action Replay codes. That, to me, was perfect - the extent of the socialization I needed in my little universe of video games - maybe a quick email to an author to get clarification on some information, or a quick post on the related forum for that game after a quick run to the search bar to see if my question had already been asked.

How is this different from 2016? Go and pull up a game specific subreddit (or subverse, if there's an active enough specific one you can think of here) and look at the content. Long winded opinion pieces, slapfights over what is and isn't an acceptable tactic/weapon/glitch, rambling YouTube wannabe's garbling on and on and on while recording gameplay footage, twitch streamer chatrooms filled with inane banter and retarded memes, and just a general cacophony, a background din of energy draining social interaction flooding every channel of information with extrovert personalities. Trying to find a nugget of useful information about a game is tiring and frustrating when every extrovert with an internet connection wants their 15 minutes of telegaming fame, and has no shame promoting themselves in every nook and cranny that'll accept a hyperlink. Want to look up where to find, say, a specific weapon in Dark Souls? Good luck finding a location that's not in some nasally YouTube kid's video.

I'm not sure where else I was going with this, so I'll end my nostalgic rant here, feeling better for having gotten it off my chest.
